parts:
Hi all,

I rewrote parts of the model (see lmer vs Stan comparison) following the recommendations of Bob and Sergio. I just wanted to post the model in case there are any mistakes. I would be very grateful if Bob or Sergio or someone else could take a look and critique it. Here it is (I had already posted the data earlier):

https://gist.github.com/vasishth/8065594

I didn't get a significant speedup compared to my earlier model, so I am probably doing something wrong. One thing I didn't understand was, why do I have to declare the type of the matrix L twice, once under model under generated quantities? The compilation process returns an error if I don't do that. 

Incidentally, for my datasets (representative psycholinguistic data), for varying intercepts models with two crossed varying intercepts, Stan does outperform JAGS from the speed perspective.

--
Shravan Vasishth
Professor für Psycholinguistik und Neurolinguistik
Department Linguistik
Universität Potsdam, D-14476 Potsdam
http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth

A few quick remarks:
a) if zero is a constant, then it should be declared and assigned to in
a transformed data block;
b) if you define an Omega correlation matrix you don't need to compute
correlations, they are in Omega;
c) L is local to the model block, this is why it is not visible in the
generated quantities block (Manual, pages 231-232), but...
d) Sigma = D * R * D, so your generated quantities block should be;

cov_matrix[4] Sigma;
Sigma <- D * R * D;

I'll compile and run your model and another one modified as above as
soon as possible (I'm going out) and let you know the results.

Cheers
Sergio

... but I get an error if I run your model!

Error : Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function
model3eeca91f3a7_kliegl_namespace::write_array(d): Sigma is not positive
definite. Sigma(0,0) is 0.

As far as I can understand, this happens because:
a) the local L variable declared in the model block is not visible
outside the block (Manual, pp. 231-232);
b) the new L declared in the generated quantities block is not the same
L, but another variabile whose value is indeterminate (garbage? all
zeros? all NANs?).

Moreover if the second L was the same as the first one, since
L <- cholesky_decompose(Omega);
then
Sigma <- L * L';
would be a correlation matrix (Omega), not a covariance matrix.

I attach a modified model, kliegl2.stan. I have:
a) declared zero in the transformed data block;
b) rewritten the generated quantities block:

generated quantities {
cov_matrix[4] Sigma;
Sigma <- D * Omega * D;
}

Since you've defined a correlation matrix, you don't need to compute
correlations.

BTW, I've tried another block (kliegl3.stan):

generated quantities {
cov_matrix[4] Sigma;
for (i in 1:4) // diagonal and lower triangle
for (j in 1:i)
Sigma[i,j] <- Omega[i,j] * sigma_u[i] * sigma_u[j];
for (i in 1:3) // upper triangle
for (j in (i+1):4)
Sigma[i,j] <- Sigma[j,i];
}

but it was not significantly more efficient (just a few seconds).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] revised model with varying intercepts and slopes
parts:
The number of data points

int<lower=1> N;

should probably be lower=0. With that, you just
sample from the prior (assuming it's proper).

You should define L in the transformed parameters block and
only Sigma in the generated quantities block. Transformed parameters
are there to let you calculate and then print out (save)
values that are functions of parameters (+ optionally data).
Functions of just data should go in transformed data.

The reason is that local variables like the L in the model
are not saved. So you have to redefine the variable in
generated quantities to save it.

Rather than passing in a vector of zeroes, you can do this:

transformed data {
vector[4] mu_prior; // vector of zeros
mu_prior <- rep_vector(0.0,4);
}

You can really speed up the following significantly:

for (n in 1:N) {
mu[n] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*c1[n] + beta[3]*c2[n] + beta[4]*c3[n]
+ u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n] + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];
}

Because u and id and c1..c3 are data, you can compute a single
vector u_id_c[n] in transformed data:

for (n in 1:N)
u_id_c[n] <- u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n] + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];

and then calculate mu in a fully vectorized way:

mu <- u_id_c beta[1] + beta[2] * c1 + beta[3] * c2 + beta[4] * c3

But I wouldn't try these kinds of optimizations until you're happy
with the model. They all make it a bit less readable in my opinion.

- Bob
